planting.note: Set plugs or divisions into loose, dry, infertile dune sand in spring; seed germination is notoriously erratic in this species, so nursery-grown plugs establish far more reliably than direct seeding.

directions: Purple sandgrass is a short-lived, wiry-stemmed bunchgrass that colonizes the loose, mobile sand of back-dune flats and blowout troughs along the Atlantic coast, including the dune fields around Cape May Point and the Delaware Bayshore. In late summer its small, open, airy panicles blush a distinctive wine-purple, casting a soft haze of color across otherwise bare sand just as most other dune plants are fading. It thrives on neglect, tolerating salt spray, drought, and constant sand movement, and reseeds itself readily into fresh disturbances without becoming a nuisance elsewhere. Use it in dune restoration plantings or a dry, sandy native garden where its fleeting fall color can be appreciated up close.

planting.note: Plant plugs or rhizome divisions into loose, well-drained sand in spring, spacing them to fill interdune swales; established colonies tolerate occasional overwash and burial by fresh sand.

directions: Beach sedge forms low, blue-green tufts that knit together by short rhizomes in the damp, sheltered swales between dune ridges, a habitat distinct from the dry, exposed dune crests held by beachgrass. Its narrow leaves and inconspicuous brownish spikes in late spring give it a quiet, textural presence rather than showy bloom, making it a supporting player in dune-restoration and native shoreline plantings rather than a border perennial. It tolerates salt spray and occasional sand burial but prefers the slightly more stable, moisture-retentive sand of a swale over an open, actively eroding foredune. Once established it needs no irrigation or fertilizer and spreads modestly to stabilize loose sand between larger dune grasses.
sources: Delaware Division of Fish and Wildlife Natural Heritage Program

planting.note: Set plugs into dry to seasonally moist, well-drained sand in spring; clumps are slow to spread and rarely need division.

directions: Greene's rush forms tight, upright tufts of wiry, blue-green stems in the dry sandy swales and back-dune flats behind the active foredune, a drier niche than the wet marsh rushes most gardeners know. Small clusters of bronze-brown flowers top the stems in summer, followed by neat round seed capsules that persist into fall. Unlike spreading rhizomatous dune grasses, it stays a tidy, non-aggressive clump, making it useful for adding fine upright texture among groundcovers like beach heather in a sandy native planting. It needs no supplemental water once established and resents rich soil or heavy mulch, which encourage rot.
